mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-01.title: Equation
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-01.body:
Let $p$ be the full price. $p + 0.8p = 1.8p = 27$, so $p = 15$ dollars.

**Answer: \$15**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-01.title: Think in fifths
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-01.body:
The sale copy costs $\frac45$ of the price, so together he paid $\frac95$ of the price. One fifth is $27 \div 9 = 3$ dollars, so the full price is $5 \times 3 = 15$ dollars. (Check: $15 + 12 = 27$.)

**Answer: \$15**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-02.title: Fill the Venn diagram
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-02.body:
Let $x$ enjoy all three. Then "exactly two" regions are $5 - x$, $7 - x$, $4 - x$. All regions add to 24:
$6 + 3 + 5 + (5-x) + (7-x) + (4-x) + x = 30 - 2x = 24$, so $x = 3$.

**Answer: 3 children**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-02.title: Inclusion–exclusion
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-02.body:
The 14 "only one flavor" children leave $24 - 14 = 10$ who like two or three. The pair counts $5 + 7 + 4 = 16$ count each "exactly two" child once and each "all three" child three times. So $16 - 10 = 2x$, the extra counting of the all-three group: $x = 3$.

**Answer: 3 children**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-03.title: Triangles with a common height
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-03.body:
DEAR is $10 \times (2 + 4) = 60$. The shaded triangles all have height 2 and bases along $EA$ that together make up the whole 8-unit strip top. Total shaded area $= \frac12 \cdot 8 \cdot 2 = 8$. Fraction: $\frac{8}{60} = \frac{2}{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2}{15}$**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-03.title: Half of the strip
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-03.body:
The shaded triangles sit in the $8 \times 2$ strip; every triangle has its base on the top and apex on the bottom, so together they fill exactly half the strip: $\frac12 \cdot 16 = 8$. $\frac{8}{60} = \frac{2}{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2}{15}$**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-04.title: Complement
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-04.body:
Without the paint limit: $3^4 = 81$ ways. Forbidden: a color on 3 or 4 walls.
- All 4 the same: 3 ways.
- Exactly 3 the same: choose the color (3), the odd wall (4), its color (2): 24 ways.

$81 - 3 - 24 = 54$.

**Answer: 54 ways**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-04.title: Count the patterns directly
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-04.body:
Allowed color counts are $2+2$ or $2+1+1$.
- $2+2$: choose the two colors (3), choose which 2 walls get the first one ($\binom42 = 6$): 18.
- $2+1+1$: choose the doubled color (3), its walls (6), and arrange the other two colors on the last two walls (2): 36.

$18 + 36 = 54$.

**Answer: 54 ways**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-05.title: List the multisets
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-05.body:
With each roll at most 8, the possibilities are $\{8,8,4\}$ (3 orders), $\{8,7,5\}$ (6), $\{8,6,6\}$ (3), $\{7,7,6\}$ (3). Total $3+6+3+3 = 15$.

**Answer: 15 ways**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-05.title: Count the shortfalls
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-05.body:
Let $d_i = 8 - (\text{roll } i) \ge 0$. Then $d_1 + d_2 + d_3 = 24 - 20 = 4$ (each $d_i \le 7$ automatically). Stars and bars: $\binom{4+2}{2} = 15$.

**Answer: 15 ways**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-06.title: Half-diagonals
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-06.body:
Each side is 1 in. Half-diagonals are $x$ and $2x$ and meet at right angles: $x^2 + 4x^2 = 1$, so $x^2 = \frac15$. Area $= \frac{AC \cdot BD}{2} = \frac{4x \cdot 2x}{2} = 4x^2 = \frac45$ in².

**Answer: $\frac{4}{5}$ in²**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-06.title: Four right triangles
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-06.body:
The diagonals cut the rhombus into 4 right triangles with legs in ratio $1:2$ and hypotenuse 1, so legs $\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $\frac{2}{\sqrt5}$. Each has area $\frac12 \cdot \frac{2}{5} = \frac15$; four of them: $\frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{5}$ in²**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-07.title: Convert km/h
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-07.body:
Average speed $= \frac{1480}{18.5} = 80$ km/h. Since $1 \text{ km/h} = \frac{1000}{3600} = \frac{5}{18}$ m/s, $80 \cdot \frac{5}{18} = \frac{200}{9} \approx 22.2$ m/s. (Don't average 87.06 and 74 km/h — the trip times differ.)

**Answer: 22.2 meters per second**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-08.title: Inclusion–exclusion on a row
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-08.body:
With Greg fixed, the other six seats form a row (the two ends both touch Greg, not each other). Let $A_i$ be "pair $i$ sits together".
- $|A_i| = 2 \cdot 5! = 240$, sum $720$.
- $|A_i \cap A_j| = 2^2 \cdot 4! = 96$, sum $288$.
- $|A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3| = 2^3 \cdot 3! = 48$.

Exactly one: $\sum|A_i| - 2\sum|A_i\cap A_j| + 3|A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3| = 720 - 576 + 144 = 288$.

**Answer: 288 ways**

mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-08.title: Place the together pair
mathcounts-2026-chapter-target-08.body:
Seats 1–6 in a row. The adjacent pair occupies seats $(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,5)$ or $(5,6)$; choose which pair (3) and its order (2). The other 4 people must fill the remaining 4 seats with neither of the other two pairs adjacent.
- Pair at $(1,2)$ or $(5,6)$: remaining seats form a row of 4. Arrangements of two pairs in a row of 4 with no pair adjacent: $4! - (\text{some pair adjacent}) = 24 - (12 + 12 - 8) = 8$.
- Pair at $(2,3)$ or $(4,5)$: remaining seats are a single seat and a row of 3. A given pair is adjacent in $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ ways (2 spots, 2 orders, 2 ways for the others); both pairs can't be adjacent. So $24 - 16 = 8$.
- Pair at $(3,4)$: remaining seats $\{1,2\}$, $\{5,6\}$; adjacent seat-pairs are $(1,2)$ and $(5,6)$. Some pair adjacent: $8 + 8 - 8 = 8$, so $24 - 8 = 16$.

Total: $3 \cdot 2 \cdot (8 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 16) = 6 \cdot 48 = 288$.

**Answer: 288 ways**
